'''Helen Abbey''' (September 1, 1915 – March 4, 2001) was an American [[Biostatistics|biostatistician]] known for her research on the health effects of radiation and on infections among [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]], and for her prolific mentoring of students in statistics.{{r|inmem|sun}} She was affiliated with [[Johns Hopkins University]] for over 50 years.{{r|sun}}

==Education and career==
Abbey graduated from [[Battle Creek College]] (now [[Andrews University]]) in 1940,{{r|sun}}
and earned a master's degree in mathematics in 1942 at the [[University of Michigan]]. She became a faculty member at the [[Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health|Johns Hopkins School of Public Health]] in 1946 and, while there, completed a doctorate in biostatistics in 1951.{{r|inmem}}

At Johns Hopkins, she became affiliated with the departments of biostatistics, epidemiology, population and family health sciences, medicine, and ophthalmology.{{r|inmem}} She retired in 1999.{{r|sun}}

==Contributions==
The topics of her own research included the effects of low-level radiation on [[cataract]]s, [[skin cancer]], and other health issues, and the history of food-borne diseases among Native American populations.{{r|inmem|sun}}
One of Abbey's studies, a 1952 work on infectious diseases, has been called "the classic study" of the [[Reed–Frost model]] in small communities.{{r|selby}}

===Former students===
Abbey taught over 4000 students at Johns Hopkins and was the mentor to over 700 graduate theses and dissertations.{{r|inmem|sun}} The story went that "if you parachuted anywhere on earth, you would land within 50 miles of a former student" of hers.{{r|kkt}}

Former students of her include the following:
* [[Victor A. McKusick]]<ref name="Thomas2016">{{cite book|author=Karen Kruse Thomas|title=Health and Humanity: A History of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, 1935–1985|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EBJBDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA101|date=July 2016|publisher=JHU Press|isbn=978-1-4214-2108-7|pages=101}}</ref>
* [[Alfred Sommer]]<ref name="Thomas2016"/>
* [[Ann Zauber]]

==Recognition==
Abbey became a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]] in 1976.{{r|fasa}} She was also a winner of the [[American Public Health Association]] Award.{{r|inmem|sun}}

The Helen Abbey and Margaret Merrell Professorship in Biostatistics Education at [[Johns Hopkins University]] is named after her and Professor [[Margaret Merrell]]. Part of the initial funding for the position was funded by her estate after she died.<ref>{{cite web |title=Helen Abbey and Margaret Merrell Professorship in Biostatistics Education |url=https://professorships.jhu.edu/professorship/helen-abbey-and-margaret-merrell-professorship-in-biostatistical-education/ |website=Johns Hopkins University |date=23 June 2016 |accessdate=15 March 2020}}</ref>
